option_description: Controls whether strict ingress filtering (ACLs, firewall rules, or cloud security group inbound policies) is applied to management interfaces such as SSH (port 22), HTTPS API (port 443), web console (port 8443), Kubernetes API (port 6443), and Prometheus (port 9090) to restrict inbound traffic to designated management zone source ranges only.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the management_plane_ingress_bypass exposure immediately when this boolean is false (not input.management_interface_ingress_filter_enabled), regardless of any other setting. Without this control, any host on any network can attempt to reach privileged administrative endpoints, directly enabling T1599.001 (NAT Traversal) and T1665 (Hide Infrastructure) to bypass zone separation. A false value is an unconditional trigger for a high-criticality, score-8 exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based management hosts, list all active iptables or nftables rules on management-facing interfaces and verify INPUT chain rules restrict source addresses for management ports.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '(22|443|8443|6443|9090)'; nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(22|443|8443|6443|9090)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each management port has an explicit ACCEPT rule bound to a specific source CIDR (e.g., 10.10.1.0/24) and a corresponding DROP or REJECT for all other sources. No rule should show '0.0.0.0/0' in the source column for these ports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS environments, query all security groups attached to management-plane EC2 instances or ENIs and check inbound rules for management ports.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters 'Name=tag:Layer,Values=management' --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{ID:GroupId,Ingress:IpPermissions}' --output json | jq '.[] | select(.Ingress[].FromPort <= 443 and .Ingress[].ToPort >= 22)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All IpRanges entries under inbound rules for ports 22, 443, 8443, 6443, 9090 show specific CIDR values (e.g., 10.10.1.0/24), not 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console, navigate to EC2 > Security Groups, filter by management-plane groups, select each group, and review the Inbound rules tab for management ports.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Security Groups > [select management SG] > Inbound rules tab > filter by Port range 22, 443, 8443, 6443, 9090
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each inbound rule for management ports lists a specific CIDR as Source, not '0.0.0.0/0' or '::/0'. If any such broad source is present, ingress filtering is not effectively enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review cloud infrastructure-as-code (Terraform or CloudFormation) definitions for security group ingress blocks associated with management resources to confirm source CIDRs are explicitly scoped.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'ingress\|inbound\|from_port' ./infra/management/ | grep -E '(22|443|8443|6443|9090)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each ingress block for management ports contains a cidr_blocks or source_ranges value that references a variable or literal CIDR bound to the management zone, not '0.0.0.0/0'.

option_description: The explicit list of source CIDR ranges that are permitted in inbound firewall rules, security group policies, or network ACLs to reach management interfaces. This array should contain only the designated management zone subnets (e.g., VPN concentrator ranges, jump-host subnets, dedicated admin VLANs). The presence of 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 in this list negates the value of any ingress filtering.
security_impact: Even when management_interface_ingress_filter_enabled is true, the Rego policy raises management_plane_ingress_bypass if '0.0.0.0/0' or '::/0' appears in this array. This reflects the real-world anti-pattern of enabling a filter control but populating it with a catch-all rule, which provides no zone separation. The policy checks each entry individually, so a single overly broad CIDR among otherwise legitimate entries still triggers the high-criticality exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all unique source CIDRs from inbound iptables rules covering management ports and output them for review.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n | awk '/dpt:(22|443|8443|6443|9090)/ {print $4}' | sort -u
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of specific CIDR ranges such as '10.10.1.0/24', '172.16.5.0/28'. The absence of '0.0.0.0/0' and '::/0' in the output indicates properly scoped source filtering.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS security group inbound rules for management ports and extract all source CIDRs including IPv6 ranges.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters 'Name=tag:Layer,Values=management' --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions[?contains(`[22,443,8443,6443,9090]`, FromPort)].{IPv4:IpRanges[*].CidrIp, IPv6:Ipv6Ranges[*].CidrIpv6}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output listing IPv4 and IPv6 CIDRs for each management port. Audit for any entry equal to '0.0.0.0/0' or '::/0', which would indicate an overly permissive rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse Terraform state or plan output to enumerate all CIDR values assigned to management security group ingress rules.
how_to_obtain.command: terraform show -json | jq '[.. | objects | select(.type? == "aws_security_group") | .values.ingress[] | select(.from_port <= 443) | .cidr_blocks[]]' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON array of CIDR strings. Each entry should be a specific range. The value '0.0.0.0/0' must not appear.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host outside the designated management CIDR, attempt a TCP connection to a management port to verify that broad CIDR entries are not actually permitting access from unexpected sources.
how_to_obtain.command: nc -zv -w 3 <management_interface_ip> 22; nc -zv -w 3 <management_interface_ip> 443
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection should time out or be refused from non-management source IPs, confirming that permissive CIDRs either do not exist or are blocked at the network layer.

option_description: Indicates whether a dedicated and formally documented network segment — such as a dedicated VLAN, a distinct subnet, or an isolated VPC — has been designated as the authoritative management zone. This segment definition establishes the source of truth for what constitutes a legitimate management-plane source address and underpins the enforcement of all ingress filtering policies.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes a compound condition that fires management_plane_ingress_bypass when both management_zone_network_segment_defined is false AND management_interface_ingress_filter_enabled is false. Without a formally defined management segment, there is no authoritative CIDR to populate ingress rules with, making all zone-separation controls either absent or arbitrary. This is an architectural prerequisite: ingress filters referencing undefined or ad-hoc ranges provide weak guarantees and are difficult to audit or maintain.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review network architecture documentation, IP address management (IPAM) records, or infrastructure runbooks for a formally designated management VLAN or subnet with a specific CIDR allocation, owner, and purpose label.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented network segment entry (e.g., VLAN 100: 10.10.1.0/24 — Management Zone, Owner: NetOps) exists and specifies that this segment is reserved exclusively for administrative and monitoring traffic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query VPC subnets in AWS and check for tags or naming conventions indicating a dedicated management subnet.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters 'Name=tag:Zone,Values=management' --query 'Subnets[*].{ID:SubnetId,CIDR:CidrBlock,Name:Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one subnet is returned with a Name or Zone tag indicating 'management', a specific non-overlapping CIDR block, and is distinct from subnets tagged for production, data-plane, or DMZ zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On-premises environments: query the switch or router configuration for a VLAN with a defined management purpose and verify it has an associated SVI or subnet.
how_to_obtain.command: ssh admin@core-switch 'show vlan brief' | grep -i 'mgmt\|management'; ssh admin@core-router 'show ip interface brief' | grep -i 'mgmt'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A VLAN entry labeled 'management' or 'mgmt' is present with an active state and an associated IP interface/SVI configured with the designated management CIDR.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Azure Portal, navigate to Virtual Networks, select the management VNet, and verify that a dedicated subnet named 'ManagementSubnet' or equivalent exists with a defined address prefix distinct from all other subnets.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Virtual Networks > [management VNet] > Subnets > verify a subnet with Purpose=Management exists with a dedicated CIDR
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A subnet named to reflect its management purpose exists with an address prefix (e.g., 10.10.1.0/24) that does not overlap with application, data, or DMZ subnets.

option_description: Controls whether outbound telemetry and monitoring traffic originating from the management zone is restricted to an explicit list of pre-approved destination endpoints, such as SIEM collectors, Prometheus remote_write targets, or log aggregation endpoints. When enabled, any telemetry egress to destinations not on the allowlist is dropped or blocked at the network or application layer.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires egress_telemetry_exfiltration_path immediately when this boolean is false (not input.egress_destination_allowlist_enabled), as an unconditional trigger. Without destination allowlisting, a compromised monitoring agent or management component can establish outbound connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure, enabling T1572 (Protocol Tunneling) via the trusted telemetry channel and T1562.006 (Indicator Blocking) by redirecting telemetry away from legitimate collectors. This is a score-8 high-criticality exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect outbound firewall or security group egress rules to determine whether telemetry ports (e.g., 514/UDP syslog, 9200/TCP Elasticsearch, 4317/TCP OpenTelemetry) are restricted to specific destination IPs.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep -E '(514|9200|4317|9090|443)'; iptables -L FORWARD -n -v | grep -E '(514|9200|4317|9090|443)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACCEPT rules for telemetry destination ports list specific destination IP addresses or CIDRs (e.g., -d 10.20.5.10/32), not '0.0.0.0/0'. A final DROP rule should exist for all other destinations on these ports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS security group outbound (egress) rules for management instances and verify telemetry-related ports are restricted to specific destination CIDRs.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters 'Name=tag:Layer,Values=management' --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{ID:GroupId,Egress:IpPermissionsEgress}' --output json | jq '.[] | .Egress[] | select(.FromPort >= 443) | {FromPort,ToPort,CIDRs: .IpRanges[].CidrIp}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules for telemetry ports return specific CIDR destinations, not '0.0.0.0/0'. A rule allowing all outbound traffic (0.0.0.0/0 on all ports) indicates allowlisting is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects in the monitoring namespace to verify egress rules restrict destination IPs to approved collector endpoints.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -A 20 'egress:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each egress rule contains ipBlock.cidr entries pointing to specific collector IP ranges and includes ports. No rule should contain '0.0.0.0/0' without a named destination port restriction tied to allowlisted IPs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform operations team to determine whether an approved telemetry destination list exists and is actively maintained, and whether enforcement is at the network layer, agent configuration layer, or both.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A maintained list of approved SIEM/collector endpoints exists, corresponding firewall or NetworkPolicy rules reference those specific IPs, and there is a documented change process for adding new approved destinations.

option_description: Describes the mechanism used to validate outbound telemetry destination endpoints. 'allowlist' mode permits connections only to a predefined set of approved collector IPs or hostnames and blocks everything else. 'denylist' mode blocks known-bad destinations but allows all others by default. 'none' applies no destination filtering whatsoever. The value reflects the enforcement posture of both the monitoring agent configuration and any host/network-layer controls.
security_impact: The Rego policy raises egress_telemetry_exfiltration_path for both 'none' (unconditional trigger) and 'denylist' when telemetry_egress_tls_with_server_auth is also false. 'none' provides zero protection against data exfiltration via telemetry channels. 'denylist' is treated as insufficient alone because an attacker using a novel or ephemeral C2 endpoint will not appear on any denylist. Only 'allowlist' mode combined with TLS server authentication fully closes the egress exfiltration path against T1572 and T1562.006.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the monitoring agent configuration file (e.g., Fluentd, Vector, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry Collector) for destination endpoint definitions and whether they represent an explicit allowlist or a general output with optional block rules.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/fluentd/fluent.conf | grep -A 5 '<match>'; cat /etc/otelcol/config.yaml | grep -A 10 'exporters:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: For allowlist mode: only named, static destination endpoints appear in output/exporter blocks with no catch-all or wildcard destinations. For none mode: a general output target with no network-layer restriction. For denylist mode: filter plugins blocking specific domains with an unrestricted default output.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check network policy or firewall egress rules to determine whether the policy defaults to deny-all with explicit allows (allowlist) or allow-all with explicit denies (denylist) for telemetry traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n monitoring -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.egress}' | python3 -m json.tool; iptables -L OUTPUT -n --line-numbers | tail -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: For allowlist: the policy's default is to deny all egress, with explicit ALLOW rules for specific collector IPs. The final iptables OUTPUT rule is DROP. For denylist: specific DROP rules for known-bad IPs with a final ACCEPT all. For none: only ACCEPT rules with no DROP.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Prometheus remote_write configurations, check whether remote_write targets list explicit static URLs only (allowlist behavior) or whether the URL is dynamically resolved without network-layer restriction.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 5 'remote_write' /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: remote_write contains a static URL pointing to an approved endpoint (e.g., http://10.20.5.10:9090/api/v1/write). If the URL is a variable or external reference without accompanying network restriction, this represents 'none' or at best 'denylist' mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the OpenTelemetry Collector or Fluentd management API (if enabled) for current pipeline configuration to identify exporter destinations and any filter processors.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://localhost:55679/debug/pipelinez | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E '(exporter|destination|endpoint)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exporters reference specific approved endpoint addresses. The absence of any filtering processor before the exporter, combined with a non-specific endpoint, indicates 'none' mode.

option_description: Indicates whether outbound connections from monitoring agents and telemetry forwarders to collector endpoints enforce TLS with full server certificate validation — including CA chain verification and hostname matching. This is distinct from merely enabling TLS transport encryption; insecure_skip_verify or equivalent settings that disable certificate validation do not satisfy this control.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires egress_telemetry_exfiltration_path when telemetry_destination_validation_mode is 'denylist' AND this attribute is false. This reflects the attack scenario where an adversary redirects telemetry traffic to a self-signed or attacker-controlled endpoint: without server certificate validation, TLS encryption protects the data in transit but does not prevent the agent from sending sensitive telemetry to the wrong destination. Combined with a denylist-only egress posture, the absence of server auth leaves the exfiltration path fully open via any novel destination not yet on the blocklist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the monitoring agent TLS configuration for certificate verification settings. Look specifically for insecure_skip_verify, tls_skip_verify, ssl_verify_mode, or equivalent options that disable server certificate validation.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'skip_verify\|insecure\|tls_verify\|ssl_verify\|ca_cert\|tls_config' /etc/prometheus/ /etc/fluentd/ /etc/otelcol/ /etc/vector/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLS configuration blocks show ca_file or ca_cert pointing to a valid CA bundle, insecure_skip_verify is absent or set to false, and server_name or similar hostname validation is not disabled. Any 'insecure: true' or 'skip_verify: true' indicates this control is not met.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl s_client to test the TLS handshake from the management host to the telemetry collector endpoint and verify the certificate chain validates against a trusted CA.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <collector_endpoint>:443 -CApath /etc/ssl/certs/ -verify_hostname <collector_hostname> < /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E '(Verify return code|subject|issuer)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)' indicates the server certificate is valid, trusted, and the hostname matches. Any other return code (e.g., 18: self-signed, 20: unable to get local issuer) indicates server authentication is not working correctly.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Prometheus remote_write, inspect the tls_config section to confirm insecure_skip_verify is false and a CA certificate is specified.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 10 'tls_config' /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: tls_config block contains 'ca_file: /path/to/ca.crt' and 'insecure_skip_verify: false' (or the key is absent, defaulting to false). The absence of ca_file with no system CA bundle and insecure_skip_verify not explicitly false indicates a misconfiguration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review monitoring agent startup logs or TLS handshake logs for certificate validation errors or warnings indicating that certificate verification is disabled or failing silently.
how_to_obtain.command: journalctl -u otel-collector --since '1 hour ago' | grep -iE '(tls|cert|verify|ssl|handshake|x509)'; journalctl -u prometheus --since '1 hour ago' | grep -iE '(tls|cert|x509)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No log entries indicating 'certificate verify failed', 'skipping TLS verification', or 'InsecureSkipVerify'. Successful TLS handshake log entries referencing a verified certificate subject confirm server authentication is working.

option_description: Classifies whether management credentials, service account tokens, API keys, or certificates used within the management layer are scoped to a single trust zone or are reused across multiple distinct trust zones (e.g., the same Kubernetes service account token used in both the management namespace and the production namespace, or an IAM role with cross-account access). 'unknown' indicates the credential inventory has not been assessed for zone scope.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires shared_credential_across_zones when credential_zone_scope is 'multi_zone', and also when the value is 'unknown' combined with distinct_zones_sharing_credential greater than 1. Multi-zone credential reuse is the primary enabler of T1078 (Valid Accounts) for lateral movement: an attacker who compromises a management component obtains a credential that is immediately valid in adjacent production zones without needing to perform additional authentication. The 'unknown' state is also treated as a risk indicator because unaudited credentials may be shared without the operator's awareness.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate Kubernetes service accounts in the management namespace and check if any ClusterRoleBindings or RoleBindings in production namespaces reference the same service account.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.namespace=="monitoring" or .subjects[]?.namespace=="management") | {name:.metadata.name, namespace:.metadata.namespace, subjects:.subjects}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service accounts from the management/monitoring namespace should only appear in RoleBindings scoped to that same namespace. Any ClusterRoleBinding entry or RoleBinding in a production namespace referencing a management service account indicates multi_zone credential scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS IAM to identify roles used by management EC2 instances or ECS tasks and check whether the same role ARN or trust policy is also attached to resources in other environment accounts or VPCs.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam list-roles --query 'Roles[?contains(RoleName,`management`) || contains(RoleName,`monitoring`)].{Name:RoleName,ARN:Arn}' --output json | xargs -I{} aws iam list-role-policies --role-name {}
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Management role policies should contain resource ARNs scoped to the management account or VPC only. Cross-account trust entries (sts:AssumeRole from production account IDs) or resource wildcards spanning multiple environments indicate multi_zone scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect HashiCorp Vault policy definitions and token role configurations to verify that management-plane tokens are bound to specific Vault namespaces or policy paths that do not grant access to production secret paths.
how_to_obtain.command: vault policy list; vault policy read management-agent-policy | grep -E '(path|capabilities)'; vault list auth/kubernetes/role/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The management agent policy grants capabilities only on paths prefixed with 'management/' or 'monitoring/'. Absence of path entries for 'production/', 'data/', or wildcard '*' confirms single_zone scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the credential inventory or service account register from the IAM or platform team and cross-reference each management credential against the list of systems and zones it has been granted access to.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each management service account or credential entry in the inventory lists exactly one zone/environment as its authorized scope. Entries showing multiple zone assignments (e.g., 'management, production, staging') indicate multi_zone credential scope.

option_description: Indicates whether active technical controls — such as Kubernetes RBAC namespace bindings, service mesh authorization policies, HashiCorp Vault namespace access controls, or network policy enforcement — are in place to prevent a credential that is valid in the management zone from being presented and accepted in an adjacent zone. This is a preventive enforcement control distinct from merely documenting zone scope; the control must actively reject cross-zone credential use attempts.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires shared_credential_across_zones when zone_isolation_enforced is false and distinct_zones_sharing_credential is greater than 1. Even if credentials are intended to be single-zone scoped, without active enforcement at the authentication/authorization layer, a credential can be replayed in any zone that the authentication system serves. This enables T1078 lateral movement and T1110.004 (Credential Stuffing) across zone boundaries. Zone isolation enforcement is the technical backstop that makes credential scope policies effective.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that Kubernetes RBAC RoleBindings in the management namespace explicitly bind service accounts to that namespace only, and attempt to use a management service account token to access resources in a production namespace to confirm enforcement.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i list pods --namespace production --as system:serviceaccount:monitoring:prometheus-agent; kubectl get rolebindings -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -E '(subjects|namespace|name)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'no' returned by auth can-i confirms the management service account cannot access production namespace resources. RoleBindings in the monitoring namespace should show namespace-scoped subjects, not ClusterRole bindings with broad resource access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Istio or Linkerd AuthorizationPolicy resources in the management zone to confirm that peer authentication restricts accepted connections to principals from the management namespace only.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -A 20 'source:'; kubectl get peerauthentication -n monitoring -o yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AuthorizationPolicy source.principals or source.namespaces fields list only the management/monitoring namespace. PeerAuthentication mode is STRICT. Any policy with '*' (wildcard) in principals or an empty source block indicates zone isolation is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In HashiCorp Vault, verify that Kubernetes auth role configurations for management components bind the token to a specific namespace and service account with no cross-namespace claims.
how_to_obtain.command: vault read auth/kubernetes/role/monitoring-agent; vault read sys/policy/monitoring-agent-policy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The role definition shows bound_service_account_namespaces listing only 'monitoring' or 'management', not '*' or production namespaces. The associated policy paths do not grant access to secrets outside the management zone paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to authenticate to a production-zone API endpoint using a management-zone service account credential and verify the attempt is rejected with an authorization error.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl -n monitoring get secret prometheus-agent-token -o jsonpath={.data.token} | base64 -d)' https://<production-api-endpoint>/api/v1/namespaces/production/pods -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 403 (Forbidden) or 401 (Unauthorized) response confirms that zone isolation is actively enforced and the management credential is rejected in the production zone. A 200 response indicates zone isolation is not enforced.

option_description: Counts how many distinct trust zones (management, production, DMZ, monitoring) share a single credential or service account token, measuring the blast radius of a single credential compromise.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'shared_credential_across_zones' exposure when this value exceeds 1 and zone_isolation_enforced is false, or when credential_zone_scope is 'unknown' and this count is greater than 1. A value greater than 1 means a single compromised credential can authenticate across zone boundaries, enabling lateral movement without re-authentication and directly violating the management plane's trust separation model.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Kubernetes, list all service account token bindings and their associated RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings across namespaces to identify tokens referenced in multiple namespace-zone combinations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq '[.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, subjects: .subjects}] | group_by(.subjects[].name) | map(select(length > 1))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of service account names that appear in more than one namespace or zone-mapped binding, indicating cross-zone credential reuse.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your identity provider or secrets manager (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS IAM) to enumerate which service accounts or tokens have policies granting access to resources tagged across multiple zones.
how_to_obtain.command: vault token lookup -format=json <token> | jq '.data.policies' && aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name <role> --query 'AttachedPolicies[*].PolicyName'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy list showing resources across multiple zone tags (e.g., prod, mgmt, dmz) attached to the same credential.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview platform and IAM teams to enumerate service account inventories. Request a mapping table of each credential to the zones it is authorized to access, then count distinct zones per credential.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A spreadsheet or CMDB record listing each credential with associated zones; any row with zone count > 1 is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Terraform or infrastructure-as-code IAM configurations to count the number of zone-tagged resource groups or environments each service account role binding encompasses.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'service_account\|role_binding' ./iac/ | grep -E 'prod|mgmt|dmz|monitoring' | sort | uniq -c
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing the same credential name appearing alongside multiple zone identifiers indicate cross-zone credential reuse.

option_description: Controls whether network-level policies (Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, firewall ACLs, or iptables rules) are applied to monitoring agents to restrict both inbound and outbound traffic to only explicitly required management-plane endpoints.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'monitoring_agent_lateral_movement_vector' when this is false and agent_zone_access_scope is 'multi_zone' or 'management_and_monitoring'. It also fires 'supply_chain_implant_in_monitoring_agent' when both agent_network_policy_enforced and agent_integrity_verification_enabled are false, meaning a compromised or implanted agent has unrestricted network egress to exfiltrate data or establish C2 channels.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Kubernetes, retrieve all NetworkPolicy objects in the namespace(s) where monitoring agents run, and verify that both ingress and egress rules are present and scoped to required endpoints only.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <monitoring-namespace> -o yaml | grep -A 20 'spec:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A NetworkPolicy spec containing both 'ingress' and 'egress' stanzas with explicit podSelector and port restrictions rather than empty or wildcard selectors.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a host running a monitoring agent (e.g., Prometheus node-exporter, Datadog agent), inspect iptables or nftables rules to verify output and input chain restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E 'ACCEPT|DROP|REJECT' && iptables -S OUTPUT | grep -v '0.0.0.0/0'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output chain rules that explicitly allow only known monitoring endpoints and drop all other traffic; absence of a default-deny rule is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Kubernetes Dashboard or Lens IDE, navigate to Networking > Network Policies, filter by the monitoring agent namespace, and verify policies exist with explicit egress destinations.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kubernetes Dashboard > Namespaces > <monitoring-namespace> > Network Policies > Inspect each policy for egress/ingress rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one NetworkPolicy with a non-empty egress ruleset scoped to management-plane CIDRs or pod selectors.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From within the monitoring agent pod or host, attempt a connection to a production workload endpoint that should be unreachable to verify egress restriction is actually enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <monitoring-namespace> <agent-pod> -- curl -m 5 http://<production-service-ip>:8080 && echo 'REACHABLE - policy not enforced' || echo 'BLOCKED - policy enforced'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection timeout or refused, confirming that the policy is actively blocking unauthorized egress from the agent.

option_description: Describes the breadth of network zones a monitoring agent can reach based on its service account permissions, network interface bindings, or VPN/peering relationships — ranging from monitoring_only to multi_zone access spanning production and restricted zones.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'monitoring_agent_lateral_movement_vector' when agent_zone_access_scope is 'multi_zone' and agent_network_policy_enforced is false, and again when it is 'multi_zone' combined with agent_privilege_level being 'root' or 'elevated'. A multi_zone scope means a compromised agent has a pre-established network path into production, making it a direct lateral movement vector without needing additional pivoting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the monitoring agent's service account ClusterRoleBinding targets and associated RBAC permissions to determine which namespace groups or cluster-scoped resources it can access.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="<agent-service-account>") | {binding: .metadata.name, role: .roleRef.name, scope: "cluster-wide"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Bindings scoped to cluster-wide roles (ClusterRole) indicate multi_zone access; namespace-scoped RoleBindings limited to monitoring namespace indicate monitoring_only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network interface configuration and routing table of the agent host or pod to determine which subnets it can directly route to.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <monitoring-namespace> <agent-pod> -- ip route show && kubectl exec -n <monitoring-namespace> <agent-pod> -- ip addr show
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Routes to production or management subnets beyond monitoring CIDR blocks indicate management_and_monitoring or multi_zone scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the agent's deployment manifest (DaemonSet, Deployment) for hostNetwork, hostPID flags, and volume mounts that imply access to host-level network interfaces spanning multiple zones.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get daemonset <agent-name> -n <monitoring-namespace> -o yaml | grep -E 'hostNetwork|hostPID|hostIPC|volumes|volumeMounts'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: hostNetwork: true or mounts to /var/run/docker.sock or /proc indicate elevated scope beyond monitoring_only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query cloud provider APIs to check if the agent's IAM role or instance profile grants cross-account or cross-VPC access that would place it in a multi_zone scope.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <agent-role-arn> --action-names 'ec2:DescribeInstances' 'rds:DescribeDBInstances' --resource-arns '*' --query 'EvaluationResults[*].{Action:EvalActionName,Decision:EvalDecision}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Allowed decisions for production resource actions (RDS, EC2 in production accounts) confirm multi_zone access scope.

option_description: Captures the effective privilege level of the monitoring agent process on the host or within the container cluster, including Linux capabilities, root/non-root user context, privileged container flags, and host namespace access.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'monitoring_agent_lateral_movement_vector' when agent_privilege_level is 'root' or 'elevated' in combination with agent_zone_access_scope being 'multi_zone'. Running as root or with elevated capabilities means a compromised agent can escape container isolation, read host credentials, manipulate host networking, and pivot into adjacent zones — dramatically amplifying the blast radius of any agent-level compromise.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Kubernetes pod security context to determine the user context, privilege escalation settings, and Linux capabilities granted to the monitoring agent container.
how_to_obtain.command:
kubectl get pod -n <monitoring-namespace> -l app=<agent-label> -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"
"}{.spec.containers[*].securityContext}{"
"}{.spec.securityContext}{"
"}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A securityContext with runAsUser set to a non-zero UID, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and capabilities drop: [ALL] indicates least_privilege. Missing or showing privileged: true indicates root level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the agent host, check the actual running user and capabilities of the agent process directly using /proc or ps.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep <agent-process-name> | awk '{print $1}' && cat /proc/$(pgrep -f <agent-process-name>)/status | grep -E 'Uid|CapEff|CapPrm'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CapEff and CapPrm values of 0000000000000000 indicate no extra capabilities (least_privilege); non-zero values or UID 0 indicate elevated or root.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the agent's Helm chart values or deployment YAML for privileged, runAsRoot, or capability additions that set the privilege level at deploy time.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'privileged:\|runAsUser:\|capabilities:\|runAsNonRoot:' ./helm-charts/<agent-chart>/templates/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: privileged: false, runAsNonRoot: true, and capabilities.drop containing ALL confirm least_privilege configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the OpenShift or Rancher UI, navigate to the agent workload's pod spec and review the Security Context section for privilege indicators.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Rancher > Cluster > Workloads > <monitoring-namespace> > <agent-daemonset> > Edit > Security Context tab
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fields showing non-root user, no privilege escalation allowed, and dropped capabilities confirm least_privilege level.

option_description: Defines the access scope of API tokens, certificates, or service account keys held by the monitoring agent — from narrowly scoped telemetry_read_only credentials to broad credentials that permit write, exec, or cross-zone API operations.
security_impact: The Rego policy unconditionally fires 'monitoring_agent_lateral_movement_vector' when agent_credential_scope is 'broad', regardless of other controls. Broad credentials mean a compromised agent immediately holds keys that can mutate production workloads, create new pods in privileged namespaces, access secrets stores, or issue commands across zone boundaries — making credential scope reduction a critical control for limiting agent compromise blast radius.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all roles and cluster roles bound to the monitoring agent's service account and extract the verbs and resources to assess whether they go beyond read-only telemetry operations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<monitoring-namespace>:<agent-sa> | grep -v '^\*' | grep -E 'create|update|delete|patch|exec|escalate|bind'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty result or only 'get/list/watch' on metrics and pod resources confirms telemetry_read_only. Any create/update/delete/exec permissions indicate broad scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes authorization API to simulate specific high-privilege actions against the agent's service account to verify whether broad access is available.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:<monitoring-namespace>:<agent-sa> -n production && kubectl auth can-i exec pods --as=system:serviceaccount:<monitoring-namespace>:<agent-sa> --all-namespaces
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'no' for both commands confirms management_read or telemetry_read_only scope; 'yes' for either confirms broad scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the RBAC Role or ClusterRole YAML directly to enumerate all rules granted to the agent's service account and map them against the telemetry_read_only, management_read, or broad categories.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrole <agent-clusterrole> -o yaml | grep -A 5 'rules:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules containing only verbs: [get, list, watch] on resources: [nodes/metrics, pods/metrics, endpoints] indicate telemetry_read_only. Broader verb or resource lists indicate elevated scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the monitoring agent vendor documentation and internal runbooks to confirm the principle of least privilege was applied during service account provisioning, and verify no ad-hoc permission grants have been applied.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl describe clusterrolebinding | grep -A 10 <agent-sa>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A single ClusterRoleBinding to a narrowly scoped role without wildcards in resources or verbs confirms appropriate credential scope.

option_description: Indicates whether a distinct VLAN is configured exclusively for management traffic (SSH, HTTPS management APIs, SNMP, IPMI), fully segregating it from VLANs carrying production workload traffic and user data.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'unsegmented_management_vlan' when management_vlan_dedicated is false and management_traffic_acl_enforced is also false, and again when management_vlan_dedicated is false and management_network_micro_segmentation_enabled is false. Without a dedicated VLAN, management traffic traverses the same broadcast domain as production traffic, enabling network sniffing (T1040) of credentials, VLAN-hopping attacks, and network boundary bridging (T1599) that collapses zone separation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a managed switch or router, display the VLAN database and port assignments to verify a VLAN ID exists that carries only management interfaces with no production ports trunked into it.
how_to_obtain.command: show vlan brief && show interfaces trunk | grep -v 'none'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A dedicated VLAN (e.g., VLAN 100 named 'MGMT') with port membership limited to management interfaces only, not shared with production VLANs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review switch or router configuration files to confirm a management VLAN is defined and that no production access ports are members of the same VLAN.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 5 'vlan' /etc/network/interfaces.d/*.cfg && grep 'interface vlan' /etc/frr/frr.conf
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A VLAN interface configuration dedicated to management with no shared port mappings to production VLANs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the network management platform (Cisco DNA Center, Juniper Apstra, or FortiManager), navigate to the VLAN management section and filter by the management VLAN to confirm its port membership and purpose.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco DNA Center > Provision > Network Settings > VLANs > Filter by VLAN Name containing 'MGMT' > View Port Members
how_to_obtain.expected_output: VLAN dedicated to management with port membership containing only OOB management interfaces, console servers, and jump hosts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a production host, attempt to reach the management VLAN gateway IP to confirm isolation — a successful response indicates VLAN separation is absent or misconfigured.
how_to_obtain.command: ping -c 3 <management-vlan-gateway-ip> && traceroute <management-vlan-gateway-ip>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 100% packet loss or 'Network unreachable' from production hosts confirms proper VLAN isolation. Successful ping is a finding.

option_description: Indicates whether explicit ACL or firewall rule sets are in place that limit management protocols (SSH, HTTPS, SNMP, IPMI, RDP) to authorized source addresses and prevent these protocols from traversing production network segments.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'unsegmented_management_vlan' when both management_vlan_dedicated and management_traffic_acl_enforced are false. Even if a dedicated VLAN exists, without ACL enforcement an attacker who achieves layer-3 routing into the management zone can directly access administrative endpoints. ACLs provide the policy-enforcement layer that prevents management protocol abuse for T1040 network sniffing and T1599 boundary bridging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco IOS/IOS-XE or similar, display the ACL configuration applied to management interfaces and verify permit rules are source-restricted and management protocols are denied on production interfaces.
how_to_obtain.command: show ip access-lists | grep -A 10 'MGMT\|management' && show running-config | grep 'ip access-group'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL entries permitting SSH/HTTPS only from designated management source ranges (e.g., 10.0.100.0/24) and implicit deny-all at the end of the list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based management hosts or firewalls (iptables/nftables), verify INPUT chain rules restrict management ports to authorized source CIDRs.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '22|443|161|623' && nft list ruleset | grep -A 3 'tcp dport { 22, 443 }'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules accepting management ports only from management source CIDRs (e.g., -s 10.0.100.0/24 ACCEPT) followed by a default DROP rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect firewall policy configuration files (FortiGate, pfSense, or Palo Alto configuration exports) for policies that define source zones, destination zones, and permitted services for management traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'ssh|snmp|https|ipmi|rdp' /etc/firewall/rules.conf | grep -v 'any'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy entries showing management protocol rules with explicit source zone 'management' and destination restricted to management hosts, not 'any'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query cloud provider security group or firewall APIs to verify inbound rules for management ports are restricted to authorized management source prefixes.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters 'Name=group-name,Values=*mgmt*' --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions[?FromPort==`22` || FromPort==`443`]' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IpRanges showing specific management CIDRs (e.g., 10.0.100.0/24) rather than 0.0.0.0/0 for management ports confirms ACL enforcement.

option_description: Indicates whether a software-defined micro-segmentation policy (NSX distributed firewall, Cisco ACI contracts, cloud security groups, or Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy) is applied within the management zone to enforce east-west traffic controls that prevent lateral movement between management workloads.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'unsegmented_management_vlan' when management_vlan_dedicated is false and management_network_micro_segmentation_enabled is false. Even when a management VLAN exists, micro-segmentation enforces intra-zone controls so that a compromised jump host or management tool cannot freely reach all other management services laterally. It is the final layer preventing T1040 sniffing and T1599 boundary bridging within the management zone itself.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In VMware NSX-T, query the distributed firewall policy API to check for rules scoped to the management zone segment that restrict inter-workload traffic within the management tier.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -k -u admin:<password> 'https://<nsx-manager>/policy/api/v1/infra/domains/default/security-policies' | jq '.results[] | select(.display_name | test("mgmt|management"; "i")) | {name: .display_name, rules: [.rules[]? | {name: .display_name, action: .action, source: .sources, dest: .destinations}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Security policies with source/destination scoped to specific management workload groups and actions of ALLOW for required traffic and DROP for everything else.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Kubernetes with Calico, list GlobalNetworkPolicy or NetworkPolicy objects targeting the management namespace to verify east-west traffic controls are enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get globalnetworkpolicy -o yaml | grep -A 30 'management' && calicoctl get networkpolicy -n <management-namespace> -o yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies with ingress/egress rules restricting traffic to specific management workload labels or CIDRs, with a default-deny catch-all.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Cisco ACI APIC GUI, navigate to Tenant > Management > Contracts and verify that endpoint groups within the management zone have explicit contracts limiting allowed protocols between workloads.
how_to_obtain.navigation: APIC GUI > Tenants > <management-tenant> > Application Profiles > <mgmt-ap> > Endpoint Groups > Review Contracts tab for each EPG
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each management EPG has both provided and consumed contracts with explicit subject filters, and no 'permit any' contract is applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS VPC security group rules to confirm each management tier instance has security group rules that restrict inbound traffic to only required source security groups rather than open CIDRs.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters 'Name=tag:Environment,Values=management' --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{ID:GroupId,Name:GroupName,InboundRules:IpPermissions[*].{Port:FromPort,Sources:UserIdGroupPairs[*].GroupId,CIDRs:IpRanges[*].CidrIp}}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Inbound rules sourced exclusively from other management security group IDs (not 0.0.0.0/0 or broad production CIDRs) confirm micro-segmentation is applied.

option_description: Controls whether the orchestration controller (e.g., Kubernetes, Ansible Tower, Terraform Cloud) requires distinct, zone-scoped authorization checks before issuing commands to each managed zone, rather than using a single global credential or cluster-admin token that spans all zones.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Trust Propagation Via Orchestration Controller' exposure when per_zone_authorization_enforced is false AND the controller_blast_radius_scope is 'all_zones', or when per_zone_authorization_enforced is false AND zone_isolation_policy_defined is false. Without per-zone authorization, a single compromised controller session can issue commands across every managed zone without re-authentication, enabling transitive trust escalation and lateral movement into production data-plane zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate Kubernetes RBAC ClusterRoleBindings and RoleBindings to check whether the orchestration controller's service account is bound to cluster-admin or to zone-scoped roles only.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="<controller-service-account>") | {name:.metadata.name, role:.roleRef.name}'; kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="<controller-service-account>") | {ns:.metadata.namespace, role:.roleRef.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: RoleBindings scoped to individual zone namespaces with least-privilege roles. Insecure: ClusterRoleBinding to 'cluster-admin' or equivalent global role.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Ansible Tower/AWX organization and credential configuration files or API exports to determine whether separate credentials are defined per inventory group (zone).
how_to_obtain.command: awx credentials list --all -f json | jq '.results[] | {name:.name, kind:.kind, organization:.summary_fields.organization.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Separate machine/cloud credentials scoped per zone or inventory group. Insecure: A single credential used across all inventories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server audit log or admission webhook configuration to confirm whether a policy engine (OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno) enforces zone-boundary constraints on controller API calls.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, rules:.webhooks[].rules}'; kubectl get constrainttemplate --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Admission webhook or policy constraint that validates zone-label or namespace scope on controller actions. Insecure: No relevant webhook or constraint present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform engineering team to confirm whether runbooks mandate separate service account tokens per zone and whether token issuance is automated via a secrets manager with zone-scoped policies.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Documented procedure and automation enforcing zone-scoped token issuance. Insecure: Single long-lived token shared or no documented policy.

typical_values: false (common in early-stage clusters using cluster-admin)

option_description: Characterizes how many distinct managed zones a single compromised orchestration controller credential or session can directly reach with write or command-execution access — limited to one zone, a defined subset, or all managed zones simultaneously.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'Trust Propagation Via Orchestration Controller' when per_zone_authorization_enforced is false AND this value is 'all_zones'. An 'all_zones' value means a single credential compromise gives an attacker full command authority across every production, staging, and restricted zone without additional authentication, enabling instant, full-scale lateral movement and trust escalation from the management plane.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all service accounts used by the orchestration controller and identify which namespaces or cloud resource groups each token can write to, then count distinct zones reached.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<controller-sa> --all-namespaces | grep -E 'create|update|delete|patch' | awk '{print $5}' | sort -u
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure (single_zone): Only one namespace/zone listed. Secure (subset_of_zones): A bounded list of namespaces. Insecure (all_zones): '*' wildcard or every zone namespace listed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve all API tokens or cloud IAM keys bound to the controller and use the cloud provider's IAM policy simulator to determine the set of resource groups or accounts each token can modify.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/<controller-role> --action-names ec2:* ssm:* --resource-arns '*' --query 'EvaluationResults[?EvalDecision==`allowed`].EvalResourceName'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Resource ARNs scoped to a single account or tagged zone. Insecure: Wildcard '*' or all zone accounts listed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Terraform Cloud or Atlantis workspace configurations to determine how many zone-specific workspaces share the same provider credentials block.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'credentials\|token\|access_key' /etc/atlantis/repos.yaml /etc/terraform-cloud/; cat ~/.terraformrc
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Each workspace uses a distinct, zone-scoped credential. Insecure: Single provider credential block reused across all workspaces.

typical_values: all_zones (most common default in untuned Kubernetes clusters or shared Terraform Cloud organizations)

option_description: Indicates whether an explicit, enforced network or authorization policy boundary exists between the management/orchestration plane and each production data-plane zone, preventing the controller from being used as a transitive relay for lateral command propagation between zones.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Trust Propagation Via Orchestration Controller' when per_zone_authorization_enforced is false AND zone_isolation_policy_defined is false. Without an explicit isolation policy, there are no enforced barriers preventing a compromised orchestration controller from relaying commands from one zone to another, allowing management-plane compromise to propagate freely into all downstream production zones through transitive trust relationships.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate Kubernetes NetworkPolicies in the management/orchestration namespace to confirm egress to production zone namespaces is explicitly denied except for required control-plane ports.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <management-namespace> -o yaml; kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.egress != null) | {ns:.metadata.namespace, name:.metadata.name, egress:.spec.egress}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Default-deny egress NetworkPolicy in management namespace with explicit allow-only to required zone endpoints. Insecure: No NetworkPolicy or allow-all egress.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) AuthorizationPolicy and PeerAuthentication resources to verify that cross-zone traffic originating from the orchestration controller namespace is explicitly denied.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A 20 'action: DENY'; istioctl analyze -n <management-namespace>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: DENY AuthorizationPolicy blocking management-namespace-to-production-zone traffic except whitelisted paths. Insecure: No DENY policy or only ALLOW policies present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query cloud provider security group and firewall rule APIs to verify that the management-plane security group has no outbound rules permitting access to production-zone security groups on management ports.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=tag:Zone,Values=management --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissionsEgress[]' --output json; gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter='network=management-vpc' --format=json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Egress rules limited to specific IPs/SGs on required ports only. Insecure: 0.0.0.0/0 egress or production zone SGs reachable on admin ports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the cloud console's VPC/network security section and review the security group or firewall rule set for the management zone, confirming no permissive egress paths to production zone CIDRs exist.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → VPC → Security Groups → filter by management-zone tag → Outbound Rules tab; OR Azure Portal → Virtual Networks → management-vnet → Subnets → NSG → Outbound security rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Explicit deny or no rule matching production zone CIDRs on administrative ports. Insecure: Allow rule with broad destination or 'Any'.

typical_values: false (default in environments relying solely on application-layer controls)
true (environments using defense-in-depth with NetworkPolicy plus firewall rules)

option_description: Controls whether health-check, readiness, liveness, or status API endpoints (e.g., /health, /ready, /status, /actuator/health) require a valid credential — such as a bearer token, client certificate, or basic authentication header — before returning any response data.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Health Check Endpoint Zone Exposure' when endpoint_authentication_required is false AND the exposed_zone is not 'management' AND response_includes_internal_state is true, OR when endpoint_authentication_required is false AND exposed_zone is 'internet' or 'dmz'. Unauthenticated health endpoints reachable from non-management zones provide free reconnaissance data to an attacker who has gained adjacent-zone access, revealing internal topology, software versions, and dependency states useful for follow-on exploitation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send an unauthenticated HTTP GET request to the health-check endpoint and observe whether a 401 or 403 is returned, or whether data is returned without credentials.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -v -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<service-host>:<port>/health; curl -v -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<service-host>:<port>/actuator/health; curl -v -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<service-host>:<port>/ready
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: HTTP 401 or 403 returned without credentials. Insecure: HTTP 200 with body returned without any Authorization header.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the application framework's security configuration to verify that health endpoints are not excluded from authentication filters (e.g., Spring Security, Express middleware, Django REST framework).
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'health\|actuator\|status\|ready\|permitAll\|anonymous\|noAuth\|exclude' /app/config/ /etc/app/ src/main/resources/application.yml; cat /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/*.conf | grep -A5 'location /health'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: No permitAll or anonymous exception for health paths; auth filter applied globally. Insecure: explicit exclusion of /health, /actuator/**, or /status from authentication requirements.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the API gateway or ingress controller configuration to verify authentication policies are applied to health-check route paths.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get ingress --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.rules[].http.paths[].path | test("/health|/status|/ready")) | {name:.metadata.name, annotations:.metadata.annotations}'; kubectl get apirule --all-namespaces -o yaml 2>/dev/null | grep -A10 'health\|status'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Authentication annotation (e.g., nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-type) present on health routes. Insecure: No auth annotation or explicit auth bypass annotation on health paths.

typical_values: false (extremely common default — most frameworks exclude health endpoints from auth by default)
true (mature deployments using mutual TLS or token auth on all endpoints including health checks)

option_description: Identifies the network zone from which the health-check or status endpoints are reachable, determined by the combination of firewall rules, security group policies, Kubernetes NetworkPolicies, and service mesh access controls governing inbound traffic to those endpoints.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'Health Check Endpoint Zone Exposure' when endpoint_authentication_required is false AND exposed_zone is 'internet' or 'dmz', regardless of internal state disclosure. It also fires when exposed_zone is not 'management' AND authentication is absent AND response_includes_internal_state is true. Exposure to 'internet' or 'dmz' zones is the highest-risk scenario because it allows any adversary on the internet to reach internal diagnostic endpoints, enabling mass reconnaissance without requiring prior network access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate Kubernetes Services and Ingress resources to identify which health-check paths are exposed via LoadBalancer, NodePort, or Ingress with public IP addresses.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get svc --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.type=="LoadBalancer" or .spec.type=="NodePort") | {ns:.metadata.namespace, name:.metadata.name, type:.spec.type, ports:.spec.ports, externalIPs:.status.loadBalancer.ingress}'; kubectl get ingress --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {host:.spec.rules[].host, paths:[.spec.rules[].http.paths[].path]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Health paths exposed only via ClusterIP services within the management namespace. Insecure: LoadBalancer or Ingress exposing /health to internet-routable IPs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to reach the health-check endpoint from each network zone (internet, DMZ, production, management) using a host in each zone to map actual reachability.
how_to_obtain.command: # From internet/external host: curl -v http://<public-ip>:<port>/health; # From DMZ host: curl -v http://<service-ip>:<port>/health; # From production host: curl -v http://<service-ip>:<port>/health
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Connection refused or 403 from internet and DMZ; 200 only from management-zone source IPs. Insecure: 200 response received from internet or DMZ host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query cloud provider load balancer and security group APIs to determine the source CIDR ranges permitted inbound to the port serving health-check endpoints.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[?FromPort==`<health-port>`]' --output json; gcloud compute backend-services describe <backend> --global --format='json' | jq '.healthChecks'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Inbound rule source limited to management-zone CIDR (e.g., 10.10.0.0/24). Insecure: Source is 0.0.0.0/0 or a broad internet-routable range.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the cloud console and examine the load balancer or API gateway listener rules to identify which IP ranges and listener ports serve the health-check paths.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → EC2 → Load Balancers → select ALB → Listeners tab → View/Edit Rules → identify rules matching /health path; OR Azure Portal → Application Gateway → select gateway → Rules → HTTP Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Listener rule for /health path restricted to internal CIDR or management zone only. Insecure: Public listener with no IP restriction on health-check path.

typical_values: production (common when load-balancer health checks are co-located with application traffic)
internet (frequent in cloud-native apps with public ALB and no path-level IP restriction)
dmz (common in DMZ-hosted microservices without separate health-check port)

option_description: Determines whether the payload returned by health-check or status endpoints contains sensitive internal information such as internal hostnames, IP addresses, software component versions, dependency connection pool states, queue depths, error stack traces, or configuration values that would aid attacker reconnaissance.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Health Check Endpoint Zone Exposure' when endpoint_authentication_required is false AND exposed_zone is not 'management' AND response_includes_internal_state is true. When health endpoints reveal internal state to unauthenticated callers in non-management zones, an attacker gains a free inventory of internal services, software versions, and dependency topology — directly enabling targeted vulnerability exploitation (MITRE T1595.002) and network configuration discovery (T1016) without any additional access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve a raw response from the health endpoint and inspect the JSON or text payload for any fields containing IP addresses, hostnames, version strings, error messages, or dependency status details.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://<service-host>:<port>/health | python3 -m json.tool; curl -s http://<service-host>:<port>/actuator/health | jq .; curl -s http://<service-host>:<port>/status | grep -Ei 'version|host|ip|error|connection|queue|pool|stack'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Response contains only {"status": "UP"} or equivalent minimal payload. Insecure: Response contains version numbers, internal IPs, dependency names, connection states, or stack traces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application's health endpoint configuration to determine the verbosity level — e.g., Spring Boot Actuator exposure settings, custom health indicator implementations, or custom /health handler code.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'management.endpoint\|show-details\|health.show\|actuator\|HealthIndicator\|healthcheck' /app/config/ /etc/app/ src/main/resources/; cat src/main/resources/application.properties | grep management
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: management.endpoint.health.show-details=never or equivalent. Insecure: show-details=always or custom handler returning full component tree.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review API gateway or reverse proxy access logs to capture sample health endpoint responses and inspect whether response bodies logged contain internal state fields.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'GET /health\|GET /status\|GET /ready' /var/log/nginx/access.log | tail -50; kubectl logs -n <ingress-namespace> <ingress-pod> | grep -E 'health|status|ready' | tail -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Minimal response bodies (e.g., 'UP', '{}', '{"status":"ok"}'). Insecure: Logged response bodies containing JSON with component names, versions, or error details.

typical_values: true (very common — Spring Boot Actuator, Node.js health libraries, and custom health handlers frequently include dependency status by default)
false (hardened deployments that override default verbosity with minimal-response health handlers)

option_description: Indicates whether all network traffic crossing the boundary between the management zone and adjacent zones (production, DMZ, etc.) is duplicated and forwarded to a passive monitoring or inspection component such as an IDS sensor, network tap, or SIEM collector for analysis and alerting.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Monitoring Blind Spot At Zone Boundary' when zone_boundary_traffic_mirroring_enabled is false AND inline_inspection_deployed is false, OR when zone_boundary_traffic_mirroring_enabled is false AND boundary_traffic_logged_to_siem is false. Without traffic mirroring, covert command-and-control sessions and data exfiltration traversing the management zone boundary operate completely undetected (MITRE T1665, T1020.001), eliminating the ability to detect lateral movement originating from management-plane compromise.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query network switch or SDN controller for active SPAN/ERSPAN sessions or cloud provider VPC traffic mirroring sessions targeting the management zone boundary interfaces.
how_to_obtain.command: # AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring: aws ec2 describe-traffic-mirror-sessions --query 'TrafficMirrorSessions[*].{ID:TrafficMirrorSessionId,Source:NetworkInterfaceId,Target:TrafficMirrorTargetId}' --output table; # GCP Packet Mirroring: gcloud compute packet-mirrorings list --format='table(name,region,network,mirroredResources)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Active mirroring session with source matching management-zone boundary interfaces and target pointing to IDS/SIEM collector. Insecure: No mirroring sessions returned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect network device configurations (router/switch) for SPAN, RSPAN, or ERSPAN session definitions on the ports or VLANs carrying management zone boundary traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: ssh admin@<mgmt-switch> 'show monitor session all'; ssh admin@<mgmt-router> 'show ip traffic-export'; cat /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml | grep -A5 'af-packet\|interface'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: SPAN session defined with source port/VLAN matching management boundary and destination port connected to IDS tap. Insecure: No SPAN session or disabled session.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SDN controller or cloud network API for packet mirroring or traffic duplication policies applied to the management zone network segment.
how_to_obtain.command: # Azure Network Watcher: az network watcher packet-capture list --resource-group <rg> --output table; # Kubernetes with Calico: calicoctl get globalnetworkpolicy -o yaml | grep -A10 'mirror\|tap'; curl -s http://<sdn-controller-api>/api/v1/mirror-sessions -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Active packet capture or mirroring policy bound to management-zone subnet. Insecure: No mirror policies or all listed as disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review network architecture diagrams and IDS/SIEM deployment records with the security operations team to confirm a tap or mirror feed from the management zone boundary is actively ingested by the monitoring platform.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Diagram shows tap point at management-zone egress and SIEM confirms active feed from that sensor. Insecure: No tap point documented or SIEM shows no management-zone boundary feed.

typical_values: false (very common — traffic mirroring is frequently omitted from management zones due to perceived internal trust)
true (mature SOC environments with full network visibility requirements)

option_description: Indicates whether a real-time inline inspection device — such as a next-generation firewall (NGFW), intrusion prevention system (IPS), or deep packet inspection (DPI) appliance — is positioned in the traffic path between the management zone and all adjacent zones, ensuring every crossing packet is actively inspected and can be blocked if malicious.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'Monitoring Blind Spot At Zone Boundary' when inline_inspection_deployed is false AND zone_boundary_traffic_mirroring_enabled is false, OR when inline_inspection_deployed is false AND boundary_traffic_logged_to_siem is false. Unlike passive mirroring, inline inspection can actively block malicious traffic in real time. Absence of inline inspection at the management zone boundary means that covert C2 sessions (MITRE T1665) and data exfiltration (T1020.001) can traverse the boundary unimpeded, with no opportunity for automated interception even if signatures are available.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the routing path for traffic crossing the management zone boundary passes through an inline inspection appliance by tracing the route from a management-zone host to an adjacent-zone host.
how_to_obtain.command: traceroute -n <production-zone-host-ip>  # Run from management zone host; mtr --report --no-dns <production-zone-host-ip>; tracepath <production-zone-host-ip>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: A hop corresponding to the NGFW/IPS appliance IP appears between management-zone gateway and the production-zone destination. Insecure: Traffic routes directly from management gateway to production zone without traversing an inspection device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect firewall policy configuration on the candidate NGFW to confirm its interfaces span the management-to-adjacent-zone boundary and that IPS profiles are applied to inter-zone policies.
how_to_obtain.command: # Palo Alto: show interface all; show running security-policy | grep -A5 'management.*production\|from management'; # Fortinet: config firewall policy; show | grep -A10 'management'; # pfSense: cat /cf/conf/config.xml | grep -A20 '<filter>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: NGFW interface assigned to management zone, IPS/threat-prevention profile applied to inter-zone rules. Insecure: No inter-zone rule with IPS profile, or NGFW not bridging management and adjacent zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NGFW management API or cloud NGFW service to confirm threat prevention profiles are active on the management-zone boundary policies.
how_to_obtain.command: # Palo Alto Panorama API: curl -k 'https://<panorama>/api/?type=config&action=get&xpath=/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry/rulebase/security&key=<apikey>' | xmllint --xpath '//entry[from/member="management"]/profile-setting' -; # AWS Network Firewall: aws network-firewall describe-firewall --firewall-name <fw-name> --query 'Firewall.SubnetMappings'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Firewall policy with IPS/threat-prevention profile applied to management→adjacent zone traffic flows. Insecure: No firewall or stateless ACL-only policy with no deep inspection profile.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network topology diagram in the NGFW management console or cloud security console to confirm the inspection appliance is positioned inline (not out-of-band) on all management zone boundary paths.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Palo Alto Panorama → Network → Zones → verify management zone interface assignments → Policies → Security → confirm IPS profile on management-to-production rules; OR AWS Console → VPC → Network Firewall → Firewalls → select firewall → Firewall policy → Stateful rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure: Topology shows NGFW/IPS as the mandatory gateway between management and adjacent zones with active threat-prevention policy. Insecure: NGFW absent from boundary path or deployed out-of-band (tap mode only).

typical_values: false (common in cloud-native environments where NGFWs are replaced with security groups and no IPS equivalent is deployed at zone boundaries)
true (enterprise environments with hardware NGFW or cloud-native NGFW services like AWS Network Firewall or Palo Alto CN-Series)

option_description: Controls whether flow records, firewall logs, or full packet captures for traffic crossing the management zone boundary are forwarded to a SIEM or centralized log analysis system with active alerting rules configured against that data.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'monitoring_blind_spot_at_zone_boundary' exposure when both zone_boundary_traffic_mirroring_enabled and boundary_traffic_logged_to_siem are absent, and again when inline_inspection_deployed is absent alongside missing SIEM logging. Without this attribute set true, two of the three detection conditions in that rule become unsatisfied simultaneously, guaranteeing a blind spot finding. An attacker conducting covert C2 or lateral movement across the management boundary will go undetected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your firewall or flow exporter to confirm log forwarding is active. On a Linux-based firewall check syslog forwarding configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(siem|syslog|logserver|splunk|elastic|qradar)' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf /etc/syslog-ng/syslog-ng.conf 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more lines referencing a remote SIEM destination IP/hostname with UDP/TCP 514 or equivalent port, confirming forwarding is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Cisco firewall/router, verify logging configuration and that the SIEM is a configured host.
how_to_obtain.command: show logging | grep -E '(Logging to|trap|host|SIEM)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'Logging to <SIEM-IP>' with an active state and appropriate severity trap level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to your SIEM console (Splunk, Elastic SIEM, QRadar, Sentinel). Navigate to Data Sources or Inputs and confirm a source is ingesting management-zone firewall/flow data. Then check Detection Rules or Correlation Rules to confirm at least one rule is scoped to management zone ingress/egress traffic.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Web UI → Settings → Data Inputs (or Data Sources) → filter by management zone firewall hostname → verify last event timestamp is recent; then Detections → Rules → filter tag 'management' or source zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Data source shows a last-seen timestamp within the expected log interval; at least one active alerting rule references the management zone firewall or boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Splunk REST API to confirm the management-zone firewall index is receiving events within the last hour.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/services/search/jobs/export?search=index%3Dmgmt_fw+earliest%3D-1h&output_mode=json'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing event results with sourcetype matching firewall logs; empty results indicate no recent ingestion.
