option_description: Indicates whether an out-of-band management channel such as IPMI, iDRAC, BMC, or serial-over-LAN is active and network-accessible on the management boundary, providing a hardware-level administrative path independent of the production OS.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'out_of_band_channel_unmonitored' is conditioned entirely on oob_channel_enabled == true. When this is true and either logging, network isolation, or strong authentication is absent, the exposure fires. OOB channels bypass standard OS-level controls and can be exploited for persistent access, making their presence a prerequisite to all three sub-conditions of the rule. If the channel is enabled but unmanaged, it represents an unmonitored administrative vector into every host on the management boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ipmitool to detect an active IPMI/BMC interface on the local host.
how_to_obtain.command: ipmitool lan print 2>/dev/null || echo 'IPMI not reachable or not installed'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output displaying IP Address, MAC, and channel information confirms an active BMC interface. 'Could not open device' or no output means IPMI is not accessible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan the dedicated OOB management network segment for active IPMI/iDRAC/BMC listeners on port 623 (IPMI over LAN) and 443 (iDRAC/iLO web interface).
how_to_obtain.command: nmap -p 623,443,80,22 --open -sV <oob_network_cidr> -oN oob_scan_results.txt
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Hosts responding on port 623/UDP indicate active IPMI. Hosts on 443 with iDRAC/iLO banners confirm Dell/HP OOB management is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Dell iDRAC, use racadm to check if the iDRAC network interface is enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: racadm get iDRAC.NIC.Enable
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'iDRAC.NIC.Enable = 1' confirms the interface is enabled; '0' means disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the server's BMC web interface (iDRAC, iLO, ILOM) by browsing to its IP address. The fact that the login page loads confirms the OOB channel is enabled and network-accessible.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Browser → https://<bmc-ip> → login page confirms OOB channel active; navigate to Network → NIC Settings to verify IP configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A login prompt or dashboard confirms the OOB channel is enabled and reachable.

option_description: Controls whether authentication attempts, session activity, and administrative commands executed over the OOB management channel (IPMI, iDRAC, BMC, SOL) are captured and forwarded to a centralized logging system or SIEM for audit and detection purposes.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'out_of_band_channel_unmonitored' fires when oob_channel_enabled is true and oob_traffic_logging_enabled is false. Because OOB channels bypass standard network monitoring paths, they represent a detection gap by default. An attacker exploiting an unmonitored iDRAC can install firmware implants, reset credentials, or pivot laterally with no log trail. This attribute being false means administrative actions on the most privileged hardware interface are completely invisible to SOC analysts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check iDRAC syslog forwarding configuration via racadm to confirm remote logging is configured.
how_to_obtain.command: racadm get idrac.syslog.server1 && racadm get idrac.syslog.enable
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'idrac.syslog.Server1 = <SIEM-IP>' and 'idrac.syslog.Enable = Enabled' confirm logging is forwarded. Empty server field or Disabled state indicates no logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For IPMI, check if the BMC is configured to send SEL (System Event Log) or audit events to a remote syslog server using ipmitool.
how_to_obtain.command: ipmitool lan alert print 1 2>/dev/null; ipmitool sel list 2>/dev/null | tail -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert destination IP matching the SIEM confirms forwarding. Absence of any remote destination indicates events are only stored locally.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the iDRAC or iLO web interface, navigate to the remote logging or syslog settings and verify a remote server is configured with an appropriate log severity level.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iDRAC GUI → Configuration → System Settings → Remote Syslog → verify 'Remote Syslog Enabled' is checked and Remote Server 1 contains the SIEM IP.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Remote Syslog shows 'Enabled' with a populated SIEM destination address.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the SIEM, search for recent events originating from OOB management interface IP addresses to confirm log delivery is occurring.
how_to_obtain.command: grep '<bmc-ip>' /var/log/syslog 2>/dev/null || curl -sk -u admin:$PASS 'https://<splunk>:8089/services/search/jobs/export?search=src%3D<bmc-ip>&output_mode=json'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Events from the BMC IP appearing in the SIEM within the expected interval confirm OOB traffic logging is active.

option_description: Controls whether the out-of-band management network is placed on a dedicated, isolated VLAN or physical network segment with enforced ingress/egress ACLs that prevent traffic from flowing between the OOB segment and production or data-plane zones.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'out_of_band_channel_unmonitored' fires when oob_channel_enabled is true and oob_network_segment_isolated is false. Without isolation, BMC/iDRAC interfaces may be reachable from production VLANs or even the internet, allowing an attacker who compromises a production workload to reach hardware-level management interfaces directly. OOB channels have elevated trust by design; an unisolated OOB segment collapses the boundary between production and hardware management completely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Cisco switch, verify the VLAN assignment of OOB management interfaces and confirm no shared interfaces exist with production VLANs.
how_to_obtain.command: show vlan brief | grep -E '(mgmt|oob|ipmi|bmc)' && show interfaces trunk
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OOB VLAN appears in the VLAN table with a dedicated VLAN ID not shared with any production VLAN. Trunk output should not show OOB VLAN bridged to production switches.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect firewall ACLs or iptables rules on the management boundary device to confirm that cross-zone traffic between OOB and production segments is denied.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L FORWARD -n -v | grep -E '(<oob_cidr>|<prod_cidr>)' || firewall-cmd --list-all-zones 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DROP or REJECT rules present for traffic between OOB CIDR and production CIDRs. Absence of any rules between these ranges is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the switch or router configuration file for VLAN definitions and inter-VLAN routing policies covering OOB interfaces.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A5 -i 'vlan\|oob\|ipmi\|bmc' /etc/network/interfaces /etc/network/interfaces.d/* 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OOB interface bound to a dedicated VLAN with no routing entries pointing toward production subnets.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a connection from a production zone host to the OOB management IP of a server to verify network isolation blocks the path.
how_to_obtain.command: nc -zv -w3 <bmc-ip> 623 2>&1; ping -c3 -W2 <bmc-ip>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timeout from a production zone host confirms the OOB segment is isolated. Successful connection is a finding.

option_description: Defines the authentication mechanism enforced on the out-of-band management channel, ranging from no authentication through default factory credentials, local accounts only, up to multi-factor authentication enforcement.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'out_of_band_channel_unmonitored' fires when oob_channel_enabled is true and oob_authentication_method is in ['none', 'default_credentials']. These two values represent the weakest authentication states: no credential requirement at all, or unchanged factory defaults which are publicly documented. An attacker who reaches the OOB network can gain full hardware-level control—power cycling, OS reinstallation, credential reset—without needing to exploit any vulnerability. Even 'local_only' without MFA carries risk if credentials are shared or weak; only 'mfa_enforced' eliminates the exposure condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to authenticate to IPMI using the known default credential pair (ADMIN/ADMIN or root/calvin) to detect unchanged factory defaults.
how_to_obtain.command: ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc-ip> -U ADMIN -P ADMIN chassis status 2>&1 | grep -E '(Get|Error|power)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful chassis status response confirms default credentials are in use (finding: default_credentials). An authentication error confirms they have been changed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Dell iDRAC, retrieve the current authentication configuration including whether two-factor authentication is enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: racadm get iDRAC.Users.2 && racadm get iDRAC.TwoFactorAuth
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'iDRAC.TwoFactorAuth.Enable = Enabled' maps to mfa_enforced. Default Password='calvin' unchanged maps to default_credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the BMC web interface and navigate to User Management and Authentication settings to inspect configured authentication policies.
how_to_obtain.navigation: iDRAC GUI → iDRAC Settings → User Authentication → check 'Two-Factor Authentication' toggle; iLO GUI → Security → Login Security → review authentication method.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MFA toggle enabled maps to mfa_enforced. Only local user list without MFA maps to local_only. Default admin account with factory password maps to default_credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the infrastructure team to determine the authentication policy for OOB management interfaces and request evidence of MFA enrollment records or PAM integration documentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation showing MFA solution (RSA, RADIUS+OTP, or certificate-based) integrated with BMC authentication confirms mfa_enforced. Absence of such documentation suggests local_only or weaker.

option_description: Controls whether cryptographic signature or hash verification is enforced for monitoring agent binaries and their updates before installation or execution, ensuring that only vendor-signed or organization-approved agent software runs in the management zone.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'supply_chain_implant_in_monitoring_agent' fires when agent_integrity_verification_enabled is false alongside either agent_network_policy_enforced being false or agent_runtime_behavior_monitored being false. Without integrity verification, a tampered or substituted agent binary can be installed silently through the deployment pipeline. Because monitoring agents run with elevated privileges and network access across zones, a compromised agent provides an ideal covert egress path from within the trusted management zone, bypassing boundary controls that treat agent traffic as legitimate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check deployment pipeline configuration (Ansible, Chef, Puppet, or custom scripts) for GPG or hash verification steps before agent installation.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE '(gpg|sha256sum|sha512sum|verify|checksum|signature)' /etc/ansible/roles/ /opt/chef/cookbooks/ /etc/puppet/manifests/ /usr/local/bin/install_agent* 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines referencing gpg --verify, sha256sum -c, or equivalent checksum validation steps before agent binary execution confirm integrity verification is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the package manager or agent-specific configuration for signature enforcement settings.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99security 2>/dev/null; cat /etc/yum.conf | grep -E '(gpgcheck|repo_gpgcheck)'; rpm --checksig $(which <agent-binary>) 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'gpgcheck=1' and 'repo_gpgcheck=1' in yum.conf, or 'APT::Get::AllowUnauthenticated "false"' in apt config confirms package-level signature checking. rpm --checksig returning 'OK' confirms agent binary signature.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For containerized agents, inspect the image pull policy and verify that image signing (Docker Content Trust or Cosign) is enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: echo $DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST; cosign verify <agent-image>:<tag> --certificate-identity-regexp='.*' --certificate-oidc-issuer-regexp='.*' 2>&1 | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 or successful cosign verify output confirms image signing enforcement. Unset variable or verify failure indicates no integrity checking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the deployment runbook or CI/CD pipeline definition for the monitoring agent and verify a mandatory signature verification gate exists before the deploy stage.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A pipeline stage labeled 'verify', 'sign-check', or equivalent with a GPG/cosign/hash validation step before deployment confirms the control is in place.

option_description: Controls whether runtime behavioral monitoring—such as eBPF-based syscall tracing, EDR agents, Falco rules, or auditd policies—is applied specifically to monitoring agent processes to detect unexpected outbound network connections, file access outside expected paths, or privilege escalation attempts.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'supply_chain_implant_in_monitoring_agent' fires when agent_runtime_behavior_monitored is false alongside either agent_integrity_verification_enabled being false or agent_network_policy_enforced being false. Even if integrity verification catches tampered binaries at install time, a legitimate-but-compromised vendor update can introduce malicious behavior post-installation. Runtime monitoring is the compensating control that detects behavioral anomalies after the agent is already running, such as a monitoring process initiating connections to external IPs or reading credential files outside its normal operating scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for active Falco rules targeting the monitoring agent process by name.
how_to_obtain.command: falco --list 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'agent\|monitor\|collector'; cat /etc/falco/rules.d/*.yaml 2>/dev/null | grep -A5 'proc.name\|container.image' | grep -i 'agent'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Falco rules referencing the agent process name with conditions detecting unexpected network connections or file reads confirm runtime monitoring is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify auditd rules are configured to monitor the agent process binary and its syscalls.
how_to_obtain.command: auditctl -l 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(<agent-binary-path>|execve|connect|open)'; cat /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules | grep '<agent-binary>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Audit rules with '-w <agent-path> -p rwxa' or '-a always,exit -F exe=<agent-path>' confirm syscall-level monitoring. No matching rules is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if an EDR agent is active on the host and whether it has a policy applied to monitor specific process behaviors.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl status falcon-sensor crowdstrike-sensor sentinelone 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(Active|running)'; ps aux | grep -E '(falcon|sentinel|crowdstrike|cylance|edr)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active EDR service with a running process confirms a behavioral monitoring capability is present. Verify through EDR console that the monitoring agent process is in scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the EDR management console or Falco/Sysdig dashboard, search for alerts or detections scoped to the monitoring agent process name within the last 30 days to confirm the process is actively monitored.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console → Device → <host> → Process Activity → filter by <agent-process-name> → confirm events are being collected; OR Falco/Sysdig UI → Policies → confirm rule targeting agent process exists and is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Process events for the monitoring agent visible in the EDR timeline, or an active policy in Falco targeting the agent process.

option_description: Specifies the Istio PeerAuthentication policy mode applied to sidecar proxies in the management zone namespace, controlling whether mutual TLS is strictly required (STRICT), optionally used (PERMISSIVE), explicitly disabled (DISABLE), or inherits from a parent policy (UNSET).
security_impact: The Rego rule 'overpermissive_service_mesh_sidecar_in_management_zone' fires directly when mtls_peer_authentication_mode is PERMISSIVE or DISABLE. In PERMISSIVE mode, the sidecar accepts both mTLS and plaintext connections, meaning any workload from an adjacent zone—including untrusted zones—can communicate with management services without a valid certificate. DISABLE removes mTLS entirely. Both conditions allow east-west traffic from untrusted zones to reach privileged management services, collapsing the service mesh boundary that should enforce zero-trust between zones. The default value in the schema is PERMISSIVE, meaning newly deployed namespaces are vulnerable unless explicitly hardened to STRICT.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve PeerAuthentication resources from the management namespace and inspect the mTLS mode.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get peerauthentication -n <management-namespace> -o yaml | grep -A5 'mtls:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'mode: STRICT' confirms enforcement. 'mode: PERMISSIVE', 'mode: DISABLE', or no PeerAuthentication resource (inheriting mesh default) are findings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a mesh-wide PeerAuthentication policy exists in the istio-system namespace that could override namespace-level settings.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get peerauthentication -n istio-system -o yaml; kubectl get peerauthentication --all-namespaces -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,MODE:.spec.mtls.mode'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A mesh-wide policy with mode: STRICT in istio-system that is not overridden at the management namespace level is acceptable. Absence of any STRICT policy at either level is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use istioctl to analyze the effective PeerAuthentication configuration for a specific management-zone workload.
how_to_obtain.command: istioctl authn tls-check <management-pod-name>.<management-namespace> 2>/dev/null | column -t
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'STRICT' in the 'SERVER' column for all management namespace services confirms mTLS is enforced end-to-end. 'PERMISSIVE' or 'DISABLE' in that column is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server for PeerAuthentication resources in the management namespace to inspect the current configuration programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://<k8s-api>/apis/security.istio.io/v1beta1/namespaces/<management-namespace>/peerauthentications | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A3 'mtls'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing 'mode': 'STRICT' under the mtls spec of the PeerAuthentication resource. Absence of the resource or PERMISSIVE/DISABLE mode is a finding.

option_description: Controls which Kubernetes namespaces are explicitly permitted to send inbound traffic to service mesh sidecar proxies running within the management zone, as defined by Istio AuthorizationPolicy resources. An empty list or absent policy results in an implicit allow-all posture.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags an exposure when mtls_peer_authentication_mode is STRICT but authorization_policy_source_namespaces is empty and no cross-zone deny policy exists. This combination means mTLS encryption is enforced but any authenticated namespace—including untrusted production or DMZ namespaces—can reach management-zone services. An attacker who compromises a workload in any namespace can pivot laterally into the management plane using the mesh's transitive trust.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve all AuthorizationPolicy resources from the management namespace and extract the source namespace lists from each rule's from.source.namespaces field.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n <management-namespace> -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{range .spec.rules[*]}{range .from[*]}{.source.namespaces}{"\n"}{end}{end}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of policy names each followed by their permitted source namespace arrays, e.g. ["monitoring", "ops"]. An empty output or missing entries indicates no source restrictions are defined.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Export the full YAML of all AuthorizationPolicy objects in the management namespace for manual inspection of every rule block, including action type and source conditions.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n <management-namespace> -o yaml > mgmt_authz_policies.yaml && grep -A 10 'source:' mgmt_authz_policies.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: YAML output showing spec.rules[].from[].source.namespaces populated with a restrictive list. An absent namespaces key or empty array is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server directly to enumerate AuthorizationPolicy objects and their source namespace fields without requiring kubectl context.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://<kube-apiserver>/apis/security.istio.io/v1beta1/namespaces/<management-namespace>/authorizationpolicies | jq '.items[].spec.rules[].from[].source.namespaces'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON arrays of permitted namespaces per policy rule. A null or empty array result confirms an allow-all condition requiring remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If using a service mesh management console such as Kiali, navigate to the Istio Config section, filter by AuthorizationPolicy in the management namespace, and inspect each policy's source namespace restrictions under the Rules tab.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali UI → Istio Config → Namespace: <management-namespace> → Kind: AuthorizationPolicy → Select each policy → Rules → From → Source → Namespaces
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each policy should display a non-empty namespace list. Policies showing no source restrictions are a finding.

typical_values: []  # absent or empty — allow-all, commonly found in default installations

option_description: Indicates whether at least one Istio AuthorizationPolicy with action: DENY exists in the management namespace that explicitly blocks inbound connections originating from namespaces outside the designated management zone. The absence of such a policy means cross-zone traffic is implicitly permitted when no ALLOW policy is scoped to restrict sources.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the overpermissive_service_mesh_sidecar_in_management_zone exposure when mtls_peer_authentication_mode is STRICT but authorization_policy_source_namespaces is empty and cross_zone_deny_policy_present is false. Without an explicit DENY policy, relying solely on ALLOW policies creates a gap: any namespace not covered by an ALLOW rule falls through to the mesh default, which in permissive configurations allows traffic. An explicit DENY ensures that even if an ALLOW policy is misconfigured or absent, cross-zone traffic is blocked by default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for AuthorizationPolicy resources in the management namespace that carry an explicit DENY action targeting source namespaces outside the management zone.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n <management-namespace> -o yaml | grep -B 5 -A 20 'action: DENY'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more policy blocks with action: DENY and a from.source.namespaces list referencing non-management namespaces. No output means no DENY policy exists, which is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use a targeted jsonpath query to list only the names of AuthorizationPolicies in the management namespace that have action set to DENY.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n <management-namespace> -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.spec.action=="DENY")]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more policy names printed. An empty result confirms no DENY policy is present and this attribute should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API for AuthorizationPolicy objects and filter client-side for DENY action using jq to confirm the presence or absence of cross-zone deny policies.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://<kube-apiserver>/apis/security.istio.io/v1beta1/namespaces/<management-namespace>/authorizationpolicies | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.action == "DENY")] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer greater than 0 confirms at least one DENY policy exists (true). A result of 0 confirms the absence of any deny policy (false).

typical_values: false  # default — no explicit deny policy, common in default Istio installations
true  # explicit DENY policy in place, expected in hardened environments

option_description: Enumerates the set of deprecated or insecure management protocols—such as Telnet (TCP/23), SNMPv1/v2c (UDP/161), HTTP (TCP/80), rsh (TCP/514), and rlogin (TCP/513)—that are explicitly permitted by firewall rules on the management zone boundary. Any protocol appearing in this list represents an unencrypted or weakly authenticated administrative access path.
security_impact: The Rego policy unconditionally fires the stale_firewall_rule_permitting_legacy_management_access exposure whenever count(input.legacy_management_protocols_permitted) > 0. These protocols transmit credentials and commands in cleartext or with negligible authentication, enabling credential harvesting, session hijacking, and command injection by any attacker with network adjacency to the management boundary. The presence of even one legacy protocol entry is sufficient to trigger the finding regardless of other controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate firewall rules on a Linux-based management boundary host and filter for rules that permit well-known legacy management protocol ports.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E ':(23|80|161|513|514)[[:space:]]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any matching lines indicate an ACCEPT rule for Telnet, HTTP, rsh, rlogin, or SNMP. No output means none of these ports are permitted at the kernel firewall layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-managed firewalls or security groups, use the AWS CLI to list inbound rules for the management zone security group and filter for legacy protocol ports.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <management-sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[?contains(`[23,80,161,513,514]`, ToPort)]' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty JSON array [] confirms no legacy protocol ports are permitted. Any populated entries identify the specific protocols that must be added to the legacy_management_protocols_permitted list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review on-premises firewall ruleset export files and grep for protocol identifiers corresponding to legacy management ports.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'telnet|snmp|rsh|rlogin|"port":[[:space:]]*(23|80|161|513|514)' /etc/firewall/rules.conf
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any matched lines identify permitted legacy protocols. A clean (no-match) result means none are explicitly allowed in the configuration file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform an active port scan from outside the management zone targeting the management boundary's ingress IP to verify which legacy protocol ports are actually reachable.
how_to_obtain.command: nmap -sS -p 23,80,161,513,514 --open <management-boundary-ip>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All scanned ports should show 'filtered' or 'closed'. Any port reported as 'open' corresponds to a permitted legacy protocol that must be added to the attribute list.

typical_values: ["telnet"]  # single legacy protocol, often from embedded device management
["SNMPv1", "SNMPv2c"]  # common in environments with legacy network hardware
["telnet", "HTTP", "SNMPv1", "SNMPv2c", "rsh"]  # heavily degraded posture, inherited from legacy infrastructure

option_description: Indicates whether any ingress firewall rules on the management zone boundary reference source IP ranges that are no longer operationally justified, including CIDRs from decommissioned systems, former vendor or contractor networks, over-broad ranges such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, or historical subnet allocations that have been reassigned or retired. A true value means at least one such range exists in the active ruleset.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the stale_firewall_rule_permitting_legacy_management_access exposure when stale_source_ranges_permitted is true. Overly broad or stale source CIDRs effectively nullify zone boundary enforcement by granting ingress rights to hosts that should have no management access. Decommissioned IP ranges are particularly dangerous because those addresses may be reallocated to untrusted or external parties, granting them inherited management access. The 0.0.0.0/0 case is a direct analogue to disabling the ingress filter entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all ingress rules for the management zone security group and identify any that use wildcard CIDR ranges indicating an allow-all source condition.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <management-sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[].IpRanges[].CidrIp' --output text | grep -E '^0\.0\.0\.0/0$'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output is the desired result. The string 0.0.0.0/0 appearing in output confirms the attribute should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all permitted source CIDRs from the management zone firewall and compare them against the current IP Address Management (IPAM) database or network topology document to identify ranges no longer in operational use.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids <management-sg-id> --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[].IpRanges[].CidrIp' --output text > current_cidrs.txt && comm -23 <(sort current_cidrs.txt) <(sort active_operational_cidrs.txt)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines printed by comm represent CIDRs present in the firewall but absent from the operational IPAM baseline, indicating stale ranges. An empty output means all permitted ranges are still operationally justified.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the firewall configuration export and check each source IP range entry against current network documentation to identify decommissioned or overly broad entries.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'source|src|from' /etc/firewall/rules.conf | grep -E '(0\.0\.0\.0/0|::/0|10\.|192\.168\.|172\.)' | awk '{print $NF}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists all source CIDRs currently permitted. Each must be cross-referenced with current network topology. Wildcards or unknown ranges indicate the attribute should be true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network security team or review change management records to determine whether each permitted source CIDR was formally approved and whether the originating business requirement still exists for each range.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Change Management System → Search firewall change tickets for <management-zone-firewall-id> → Review source CIDR justifications → Cross-reference with current asset inventory and vendor/contractor contracts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each permitted CIDR should have an active, documented business justification. Ranges without current tickets or with closed/expired justifications confirm stale_source_ranges_permitted should be set to true.

typical_values: false  # all permitted source ranges are documented and operationally current
true  # at least one stale or overly broad range present, common in mature environments with accumulated technical debt

option_description: Records the integer number of calendar days elapsed since the management zone firewall rules were last formally reviewed, validated against current operational requirements, and approved by an authorized owner. This metric drives the governance dimension of the stale firewall rule assessment and is derived from change management logs or firewall audit records.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the stale_firewall_rule_permitting_legacy_management_access exposure when last_rule_review_days_ago exceeds 365. An annual threshold reflects the minimum acceptable governance cadence; rules that have not been reviewed in over a year are likely to contain entries from personnel transitions, decommissioned systems, or expired vendor relationships that no longer have operational justification. Even if no legacy protocols or stale CIDRs are currently present, an unreviewed ruleset cannot provide assurance that drift has not occurred since the last review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the firewall platform's built-in audit log or change history for the management zone ruleset to identify the timestamp of the most recent review or approval event.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'review\|approved\|audit\|accepted' /var/log/firewall/management-zone-audit.log | tail -20 | awk '{print $1, $2}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A timestamp on or near a recent date, e.g. '2024-11-15 14:32:00'. Calculate days_elapsed = (today - that date). A timestamp older than 365 days is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud environments, use the AWS Config or CloudTrail API to retrieve the last modification or formal review event associated with the management security group.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=<management-sg-id> --query 'Events[?contains(EventName,`Authorize`) || contains(EventName,`Revoke`)].{Time:EventTime,Event:EventName}' --output table | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table showing the most recent Authorize/Revoke event with its timestamp. Note that a last-change event is not equivalent to a formal review; use this as a lower bound and supplement with process_audit steps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the most recent firewall rule review sign-off document or ticket from the network security or change management team and calculate the elapsed days from the approval date to today.
how_to_obtain.command: python3 -c "from datetime import date; review=date(YYYY,MM,DD); print((date.today()-review).days)"
how_to_obtain.navigation: Change Management System → Search for 'management zone firewall review' → Sort by date descending → Open most recent closed ticket → Note the approval/closure date
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing elapsed days. Values above 365 trigger the Rego exposure. Values above 180 should be flagged as approaching the review threshold.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If the organization uses a firewall management platform such as Firepower Management Center, Panorama, or Tufin, navigate to the management zone policy's audit history and identify the most recent formal review or recertification entry.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Firewall Management Console → Policy Management → Management Zone Ruleset → Audit History / Policy Review Log → Sort by Date Descending → Record the most recent Review/Approved entry date
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A visible dated entry marked as reviewed or certified. Absence of any review entry or an entry older than 365 days confirms the attribute value exceeds the threshold.

typical_values: 180  # approaching threshold, common in organizations with semi-annual review cycles
366  # just past the annual threshold, triggers the Rego exposure
730  # two years without review, common in environments with accumulated firewall technical debt
9999  # unknown or never formally reviewed, worst-case finding
